analysis.one_liner: Directed the FCC to curb radio-industry consolidation and payola, with license revocation for anticompetitive conduct.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in April 2003, sent to a telecommunications subcommittee two weeks later, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responded to what it called a crisis in radio after 1996 deregulation: the number of station owners fell from 5,100 to 3,800 in five years, and the biggest companies bought stations, managed concert venues, and promoted tours at the same time. It would have let the FCC revoke a station's license for practices that shut independent artists and promoters off the air, capped how much of the national audience and local markets any company could control, limited the short-term deals big groups use to run rivals' stations, and updated the ban on payola so stations could not take money from record companies or promoters in exchange for airplay.
analysis.who_benefits: Radio listeners, who would get more locally produced and independently owned programming; independent musicians and smaller record labels, who would gain access to airtime without paying for play; concert-goers, since the bill targeted the exclusive ties between station owners and venue operators that the bill's findings linked to concert ticket prices rising 61 percent from 1996 to 2001 while overall prices rose 13 percent; and locally owned radio stations, which would face less competition from big groups operating multiple stations in their market through local marketing agreements.

how_it_helps.text: Allowed the FCC to revoke a station's license for willful, repeated practices that significantly hinder or prevent the broadcast of programming produced or promoted by someone independent of the station owner, and for antitrust violations involving concert venues or promotion.

Directed the FCC to write rules barring station owners from pressuring artists or promoters over the price or terms of selling their music, performances, or promotion services, from discriminating against artists who refuse deals with the owner's affiliates, and from locking up artists with exclusive contracts that block other stations and venues.

Required a public hearing before approving any radio deal that would push a company's national audience reach past 60 percent, and barred transfers or local marketing agreements giving one company more than 35 percent of a local market's audience share or advertising revenue.

Prohibited a station from using its control over what gets broadcast to extract money or other consideration from a record company, artist, or concert promoter, updating payola rules that predated the new promotional practices.
Barred the FCC from loosening existing local radio ownership limits and required annual reports to Congress on industry compliance and circumvention practices.

analysis.who_pays: Large radio station groups that had consolidated hundreds of stations after the 1996 Telecommunications Act would lose exclusive contracts with artists, limits on local marketing agreements, a hearing requirement on big acquisitions, and exposure to license revocation for anticompetitive conduct. Vertically integrated concert promoters and venue operators would lose the ability to use station airplay to steer acts into their venues, and record companies would lose promotional channels built on paying stations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large radio groups and concert promoters

drawbacks.text: Revoking a broadcast license for broadly defined 'unfair or deceptive acts' is an unusually heavy sanction, and the bill itself acknowledged the FCC's rules would need to leave room for 'legitimate promotional activities' to continue — a line critics could argue the FCC would struggle to draw without chilling ordinary promotion or raising First Amendment concerns about licensed speech.

The bill imposed substantial compliance costs: stations would have to file reports on every 'special relationship contract' with other stations or their owners, and local marketing agreements covering more than 15 percent of another station's programming would be capped at one-year terms, ending arrangements that in some cases keep marginal stations operating.
The 60 percent national reach hearing trigger and the freeze on raising local ownership limits would restrict the ability of any broadcaster, not only anticompetitive ones, to grow or restructure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a well-documented problem — the bill's own findings cite a 25 percent drop in station owners, the top 50 radio groups' share of industry revenues jumping from 43.6 percent to 62.5 percent, and concert prices rising more than four times faster than inflation after 1996. The main costs fall on the consolidated companies rather than listeners. The design is not perfect: license revocation is a blunt tool and the line between a bribe and a legitimate promotion deal would fall to FCC rulemaking. But the compliance burdens are real without being disabling, and the public-facing gains — more diverse programming, access for independent artists, pressure on ticket prices — are large relative to them.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing or markup until the 108th Congress ended and the bill died.

narrative.text: Rep. Anthony Weiner introduced the bill on April 10, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On April 24, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet, where consideration ended.
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The bill's findings documented that radio station owners fell from 5,100 in 1996 to 3,800 in 2001, and that the top 50 radio groups went from owning 8.6 percent of stations and taking 43.6 percent of revenues in 1995 to 27.5 percent and 62.5 percent by 2000.

The bill cited studies showing average concert ticket prices rose more than 61 percent from 1996 to 2001, against a 13 percent rise in the Consumer Price Index, during the period of radio and concert-promotion consolidation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large radio station groups and vertically integrated concert promoters that had consolidated after 1996 kept their station holdings, exclusive artist and venue arrangements, and promotional payment channels, with no new limits and no recorded vote anyone had to answer for. The committee leadership avoided a contentious fight with an influential industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large radio groups and concert promoters

for.name: Rep. Anthony Weiner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and drafted findings tying radio consolidation and vertical integration to fewer independent voices and sharply higher concert ticket prices.

for.name: 1 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Republicans in the 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet on April 24, 2003, and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats, but it never reached the floor or a committee vote, so the record shows no partisan split on the merits.

industries.note: After the 1996 Telecommunications Act removed national ownership limits, the biggest groups went from owning 8.6 percent of stations in 1995 to 27.5 percent by 2000, and the bill would have frozen ownership limits, triggered hearings on deals pushing national reach past 60 percent, and capped local control at 35 percent of audience share or ad revenue. Their gain from consolidation came at the cost of programming diversity and independent artists' access to the air.

Radio owners had combined with promoters and venue operators, and the bill would have banned discriminating against artists who refused affiliate deals, barred exclusive contracts, and allowed license revocation for antitrust violations in concert venues or promotion. Ticket prices rose 61 percent from 1996 to 2001 while overall inflation was 13 percent, costs carried by concert-goers.

The bill would have prohibited stations from extracting money or other consideration from record companies in exchange for airplay, closing promotional channels that existed because payola rules predated the new practices. That spending exists to buy airplay rather than to serve listeners, and it crowds out music chosen on its merits.

The bill required the FCC to review within a year whether these systems, which determine what markets stations are measured in, were being manipulated by the industry, and to develop ways to measure rural and small markets the systems do not cover. Any resulting changes would have reduced the firms' unchecked role in a system that stations' fortunes depend on.
